title: The man on the road
hook: Upaka the wanderer hears him, shakes his head, and takes another road (MN 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduma: Brahma pleaded, and the Buddha saw people like lotuses at every depth. Some are ready.

Not every first meeting goes well. A pitch gets a polite nod. A favorite song gets a shrug and a huh, good for you. The subject changes, and that's that. The Buddha has decided to teach. He's thought about who should hear first, and he's chosen his five old companions, the ones who left him when he ate. They're in a deer park near Varanasi, a long walk away. So he sets out on the road, and not far along it, he meets a stranger.
screen: `HUH, GOOD FOR YOU.` → `A LONG WALK TO THE FIVE.` → `A STRANGER ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: The stranger is Upaka, a wanderer too, from a group called the Ajivikas, and he's struck by what he sees. Your face is so clear, friend, he says, your skin so bright. Who's your teacher? Whose teaching do you follow? It's an open door. The Buddha answers, the sutta says, in verse. He says he has no teacher; he found this himself. He has overcome everything, understood everything, and he's on his way to Kasi to set the wheel of the teaching turning, to beat the drum of the deathless in a world gone blind. It's a big answer. Upaka listens. Then he says something like: may it be so, friend. He shakes his head, takes a side road, and walks away. That's it. The stranger doesn't buy it. The Buddha tells this story himself, and doesn't hide it. He doesn't chase Upaka. He doesn't argue. He just keeps walking to the deer park. The later tradition adds a coda. The commentary's story goes that Upaka fell in love and married a hunter's daughter named Capa, had a son, and later, unhappy, went looking for the Buddha after all, and became a monk. Capa's own verses survive in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns. So the man on the road wasn't lost. He just wasn't ready yet.
screen: `WHO'S YOUR TEACHER?` · `NO TEACHER. I FOUND IT.` · `MAY IT BE SO. A SIDE ROAD.` · `NOT LOST. JUST NOT YET.` · then, large: `NOT EVERYONE IS READY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who disagrees with you about something that matters to you, small, like a movie, or big, like how to live, and picture them shaking their head and walking off down a side road. Notice what rises, the urge to chase, to argue, to prove, and let it be there. Then gently let them go, wish them well on their road, and keep walking yours.
Upaka. The wanderer who asked the Buddha about his teaching, then said may it be so, shook his head, and took another road.
Your line: not everyone is ready. The road to the deer park goes on. Sixty days, well walked.

howItsDone: Buddhists retell Upaka's meeting as a reminder not to force the teaching on anyone, and in some traditions teachers wait to be asked before they teach, letting people come and go freely.

fork.reveal: Upaka takes the side road. the stranger doesn't believe. and the Buddha doesn't chase him.

original.note: Pali: an Ajivika, a member of the wandering group Upaka belonged to.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone who met the Buddha was converted on the spot.
what it means: a stranger who asked about his teaching shook his head and walked away, and the Buddha let him go.
what a scholar hears: MN 26 records Upaka the Ajivika's 'may it be so, friend' (hupeyya), his head-shake and the bypath; the commentary and Therigatha (Capa's verses) tell of his later return.
recall: the tempter, whose name comes from death
awakening, like waking up from a dream

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they feel and no longer repeats day 59's 'something that changed you' setup; removed the unsourced superlatives 'the very first question anyone asks' and 'the first stranger' (MN 26 doesn't say first, and day 58's merchants came earlier); softened 'many teachers' in howItsDone.
MN 26 paraphrased: Upaka's question, the Buddha's verses (no teacher, the drum of the deathless at Kasi/Benares), 'may it be so, friend', head-shake, bypath. Confirm.
The coda (Upaka marries Capa, has a son, later ordains) is from the commentary and the Therigatha verses of Capa. Confirm details and whether to keep.
'Kasi' is the region with Varanasi (Benares); the hook says 'near Varanasi'. Confirm.

Review pass: 'the first person the Buddha ever told about his awakening' conflicted with day 58, where Tapussa and Bhallika meet him first and become lay followers (Vinaya, Mahavagga 1.4). Reworded to 'the first stranger to ask about his teaching' throughout. Confirm framing.

Review pass: howItsDone softened from 'teachers traditionally teach only when asked' (stated as universal) to 'many teachers keep the custom of waiting to be asked'. Practice varies by tradition; confirm.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
